_note: German runtime strings for the modules under www/shared/. WRITTEN, not translated: the English file is the brief, not the source text. STANDARD GERMAN, Germany-tagged (#304): written to read naturally in Germany, but deliberately without Germany-only slang and without words that split by country, so a room in Vienna, Zurich or Bolzano is not reading somebody else's dialect. That is a register rule, not a country rule. THE RULES THIS FILE SETTLES FOR THE WHOLE LANGUAGE. (1) DU to one player, IHR only where the string genuinely addresses the whole room. They are two NUMBERS, not two politeness levels, the same split neutral Spanish makes with tu and ustedes and the one French got wrong on eight strings before #238 caught it. So it is checked key by key against es, pt and fr rather than discovered by playing. (2) SIE NEVER, in game UI. German's formal pronoun is a third axis the other four languages do not have, and it would set exactly the register a party game does not want. The FAQ answers and the meta descriptions keep the PLURAL on purpose: those address a reader who is a group, and they are indexed pages rather than in-game UI. (3) NOUNS ARE CAPITALISED, so some of what #240 recorded as sentence-case taste is grammar here. A capital in the middle of a German sentence is not an error to report. (4) NO NO-BREAK SPACE. French needs one before ? ! and : and writes it as \u00a0; German does not, and copying that rule across would put invisible characters in the source for nothing. (5) THE POSSESSIVE IS AVOIDED IN {name} TEMPLATES. `{name}s Spiel` is wrong for a name ending in s, z or ß, which wants `{name}' Spiel`, and a name is arbitrary text, so the phrasing goes round it: `Spiel von {name}`, `{name} ist dran`, `{name} umbenennen`. The same move French made in #238. (6) THE VOCABULARY, settled once here: Handy not Mobiltelefon; Raum for a game room and Lobby for the lobby screen, which is one word better than French, where salon had to carry both; Runde for a round; Tipp for the hint the impostor gets and Hinweis for the clue a player says, because the two are different things and English tells them apart too; Host, not Gastgeber, because it is what German multiplayer UIs say and it fits the badge; Leinwand for the canvas in the drawing game. There is no noun for a turn: German says `dran sein`, so the turn banners are `Du bist dran` and `{name} ist dran` and no screen needs one. THE THREE GAME NAMES are a family of compounds, Impostor Wortspiel, Impostor Tanzspiel, Impostor Zeichenspiel, which is the same thing the Romance locales do with de/das/du and the shape German has for it. \n in a value is a real line break in the rendered string, not markup.
